claim: Senescent cells accumulate in fat with aging.
source: Senescent cells accumulate in fat with aging.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Tchkonia et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2015; Stout et al., 2014) in the introduction.

claim: Genetic clearance of senescent cells from progeroid INK-ATTAC mice prevents lipodystrophy.
source: We previously found genetic clearance of senescent cells from progeroid INK-ATTAC mice prevents lipodystrophy.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Baker et al., 2011) mentioned in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Primary human senescent fat progenitors secrete activin A.
source: Here we show that primary human senescent fat progenitors secrete activin A and directly inhibit adipogenesis in non-senescent progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a,b demonstrating increased activin A transcript and protein levels in senescent cells.

claim: Senescent fat progenitors directly inhibit adipogenesis in non-senescent progenitors.
source: Here we show that primary human senescent fat progenitors secrete activin A and directly inhibit adipogenesis in non-senescent progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by co-culture experiments shown in Figure 1 and conditioned medium experiments in Figure 2.

claim: Blocking activin A partially restored lipid accumulation in differentiating progenitors exposed to senescent cells.
source: Blocking activin A partially restored lipid accumulation and expression of key adipogenic markers in differentiating progenitors exposed to senescent cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing effects of SB-431542 and activin A neutralizing antibody.

claim: Blocking activin A partially restored expression of key adipogenic markers in differentiating progenitors exposed to senescent cells.
source: Blocking activin A partially restored lipid accumulation and expression of key adipogenic markers in differentiating progenitors exposed to senescent cells.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 3b,d showing increased FABP4, PPARγ, C/EBPα, and PLIN1 with activin A inhibition.

claim: Mouse fat tissue activin A increased with aging.
source: Mouse fat tissue activin A increased with aging.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c and Figure 7c showing increased activin A in old versus young mice.

claim: Clearing senescent cells from 18-month-old naturally-aged INK-ATTAC mice reduced circulating activin A.
source: Clearing senescent cells from 18-month-old naturally-aged INK-ATTAC mice reduced circulating activin A, blunted fat loss, and enhanced adipogenic transcription factor expression within 3 weeks.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4e showing reduced circulating activin A in INK-ATTAC+/- mice after AP20187 treatment.

claim: Clearing senescent cells from 18-month-old naturally-aged INK-ATTAC mice blunted fat loss.
source: Clearing senescent cells from 18-month-old naturally-aged INK-ATTAC mice reduced circulating activin A, blunted fat loss, and enhanced adipogenic transcription factor expression within 3 weeks.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4a showing less fat loss in INK-ATTAC+/- mice compared to WT mice.

claim: Clearing senescent cells from 18-month-old naturally-aged INK-ATTAC mice enhanced adipogenic transcription factor expression within 3 weeks.
source: Clearing senescent cells from 18-month-old naturally-aged INK-ATTAC mice reduced circulating activin A, blunted fat loss, and enhanced adipogenic transcription factor expression within 3 weeks.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4f showing increased C/EBPα and PPARγ expression in adipose tissue of INK-ATTAC+/- mice.

claim: JAK inhibitor suppressed senescent cell activin A production.
source: JAK inhibitor suppressed senescent cell activin A production and blunted senescent cell-mediated inhibition of adipogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5a,b showing reduced activin A transcript and protein levels in senescent cells treated with JAK inhibitor.

claim: JAK inhibitor blunted senescent cell-mediated inhibition of adipogenesis.
source: JAK inhibitor suppressed senescent cell activin A production and blunted senescent cell-mediated inhibition of adipogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5c,d showing improved adipogenesis when target cells were exposed to conditioned medium from JAK inhibitor-treated senescent cells.

claim: Eight weeks-treatment with ruxolitinib reduced circulating activin A in 22-month-old mice.
source: Eight weeks-treatment with ruxolitinib, an FDA-approved JAK1/2 inhibitor, reduced circulating activin A, preserved fat mass, reduced lipotoxicity, and increased insulin sensitivity in 22-month-old mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7c showing reduced plasma activin A in ruxolitinib-treated mice.

claim: Eight weeks-treatment with ruxolitinib preserved fat mass in 22-month-old mice.
source: Eight weeks-treatment with ruxolitinib, an FDA-approved JAK1/2 inhibitor, reduced circulating activin A, preserved fat mass, reduced lipotoxicity, and increased insulin sensitivity in 22-month-old mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6a,d and Figure 7a showing preserved fat mass in ruxolitinib-treated mice.

claim: Eight weeks-treatment with ruxolitinib reduced lipotoxicity in 22-month-old mice.
source: Eight weeks-treatment with ruxolitinib, an FDA-approved JAK1/2 inhibitor, reduced circulating activin A, preserved fat mass, reduced lipotoxicity, and increased insulin sensitivity in 22-month-old mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7e,f,g showing reduced plasma FFA and hepatic triglycerides in ruxolitinib-treated mice.

claim: Eight weeks-treatment with ruxolitinib increased insulin sensitivity in 22-month-old mice.
source: Eight weeks-treatment with ruxolitinib, an FDA-approved JAK1/2 inhibitor, reduced circulating activin A, preserved fat mass, reduced lipotoxicity, and increased insulin sensitivity in 22-month-old mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8d,e showing improved insulin tolerance in ruxolitinib-treated mice.

claim: Adipose tissue stores potentially cytotoxic lipids, including fatty acids, as less reactive neutral triglycerides within fat droplets.
source: A major function of adipose tissue is to store potentially cytotoxic lipids, including fatty acids (FAs), as less reactive neutral triglycerides (TG) within fat droplets (Listenberger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Listenberger et al., 2003 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Lipid storage by adipose tissue constitutes a defense against lipotoxicity and metabolic disease.
source: Lipid storage by adipose tissue appears to constitute a defense against lipotoxicity and metabolic disease (Wang et al., 2008; Unger and Scherer, 2010; Gustafson et al., 2015; Tchkonia et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Fat cells turn over throughout life, with generation of new fat cells through differentiation of fat progenitors.
source: Fat cells turn over throughout life, with generation of new fat cells through differentiation of fat progenitors (also known as preadipocytes or adipose-derived stem cells) (Tchkonia et al., 2013; Spalding et al., 2008; Tchoukalova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Adipogenesis is orchestrated by a transcription factor cascade involving PPARγ and C/EBPα.
source: Adipogenesis is orchestrated by a transcription factor cascade involving the two key regulators, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ) and CCAAT/enhancer binding protein-α (C/EBPα) (Wu et al., 1999; Lin and Lane, 1994)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wu et al., 1999 and Lin and Lane, 1994 and represents established knowledge.

claim: PPARγ and C/EBPα regulate downstream targets including FABP4 and PLIN1.
source: Adipogenesis is orchestrated by a transcription factor cascade involving the two key regulators, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ) and CCAAT/enhancer binding protein-α (C/EBPα) (Wu et al., 1999; Lin and Lane, 1994) and their downstream targets, including fatty acid binding protein 4 (FABP4) and perilipin (PLIN1) (Bernlohr et al., 1997; Sun, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Compromised adipogenic capacity can contribute to impaired ability of adipose tissue to store lipids, leading to FA spillover and ectopic lipid accumulation.
source: Compromised adipogenic capacity can contribute to impaired ability of adipose tissue to store lipids, leading to FA spillover and ectopic lipid accumulation in liver and other sites, insulin resistance, and lipotoxicity (Garbarino and Sturley, 2009; Slawik and Vidal-Puig, 2006; Tchkonia et al., 2006; Guo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: By late middle age, capacity for adipogenesis, PPARγ and C/EBPα expression, adipose tissue mass, and metabolic function begin to decline in experimental animals and humans.
source: By late middle age, capacity for adipogenesis, PPARγ and C/EBPα expression, adipose tissue mass, and metabolic function begin to decline in experimental animals and humans (Tchkonia et al., 2010; Slawik and Vidal-Puig, 2006; Fink et al., 1983; Tchkonia et al., 2013; Cowie et al., 2006; North and Sinclair, 2012; Palmer et al., 2015; Cartwright et al., 2007; Raguso et al., 2006; Kuk et al., 2009; Cartwright et al., 2010; Tchkonia et al., 2007; Karagiannides et al., 2001; Kirkland et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Age-related lipodystrophy likely contributes to the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction at older ages.
source: This age-related lipodystrophy likely contributes to the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction at older ages (Gustafson et al., 2015; Tchkonia et al., 2010; Tchkonia et al., 2006; Guo et al., 2007; Kuk et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents an inference based on established knowledge.

claim: Cellular senescence refers to an essentially irreversible arrest of cell proliferation.
source: Cellular senescence refers to an essentially irreversible arrest of cell proliferation (Hayflickl and Moorhead, 1961).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hayflick and Moorhead, 1961 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Cellular senescence can be induced by DNA damage, telomere shortening, radiation, chemotherapeutics, and reactive metabolites.
source: It can be induced by a variety of stresses, including DNA damage, telomere shortening, radiation, chemotherapeutics, and reactive metabolites (Tchkonia et al., 2013; Campisi and d'Adda di Fagagna, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Senescent cells accumulate in adipose tissue with aging across a number of mammalian species.
source: Senescent cells accumulate in adipose tissue with aging across a number of mammalian species (Tchkonia et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2015; Stout et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work including the authors' own studies.

claim: Senescent cells secrete an array of cytokines, chemokines, proteases, and growth factors—the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).
source: Senescent cells accumulate in adipose tissue with aging across a number of mammalian species (Tchkonia et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2015; Stout et al., 2014) and secrete an array of cytokines, chemokines, proteases, and growth factors—the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) (Coppé et al., 2008; Coppé et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cultures of progenitors isolated from adipose depots of older animals or humans contain senescent cells and exhibit impaired adipogenic capacity.
source: Cultures of progenitors isolated from adipose depots of older animals or humans contain senescent cells and exhibit impaired adipogenic capacity, with reduced lipid accumulation and C/EBPα and PPARγ expression after exposure to differentiation-inducing stimuli (Tchkonia et al., 2010; Tchkonia et al., 2007; Park et al., 2005; Mitterberger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Senescent cells appear to be able to spread inflammatory activation and perhaps even senescence to nearby non-senescent cells.
source: Senescent cells appear to be able to spread inflammatory activation and perhaps even senescence to nearby non-senescent cells (Xu et al., 2015; Acosta et al., 2013; Nelson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and represents a speculative interpretation of data.

claim: Clearance of senescent cells can delay age-related phenotypes including lordokyphosis and cataract formation.
source: We showed that clearance of senescent cells can delay age-related phenotypes including lordokyphosis and cataract formation, and can actually reverse age-related fat loss in progeroid BubR1H/H animals (Baker et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baker et al., 2011.

claim: Clearance of senescent cells can reverse age-related fat loss in progeroid BubR1H/H animals.
source: We showed that clearance of senescent cells can delay age-related phenotypes including lordokyphosis and cataract formation, and can actually reverse age-related fat loss in progeroid BubR1H/H animals (Baker et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baker et al., 2011.

claim: IL6, TNFα, and IFNγ can inhibit adipogenesis in vitro.
source: Furthermore, interleukin-6 (IL6) (Gustafson and Smith, 2006; Okada et al., 2012) , tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα) (Tchkonia et al., 2007; Gustafson and Smith, 2006; Okada et al., 2012) , and interferon γ (IFNγ) (McGillicuddy et al., 2009) can inhibit adipogenesis in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: IL6, TNFα, and IFNγ are among the SASP components in senescent fat progenitors and other senescent cell types.
source: These factors are among the SASP components in senescent fat progenitors and other senescent cell types (Tchkonia et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015; Coppé et al., 2008; Coppé et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway plays a role in regulating the SASP.
source: We recently reported that the JAK/STAT (Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription) pathway plays a role in regulating the SASP (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: Activin A is a member of the transforming growth factor superfamily.
source: We report here that senescent fat progenitors impede differentiation of non-senescent progenitors, in part by secreting activin A, a member of the transforming growth factor superfamily, which can inhibit adipogenesis and interfere with stem cell and progenitor function (Zaragosi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Activin A can inhibit adipogenesis and interfere with stem cell and progenitor function.
source: We report here that senescent fat progenitors impede differentiation of non-senescent progenitors, in part by secreting activin A, a member of the transforming growth factor superfamily, which can inhibit adipogenesis and interfere with stem cell and progenitor function (Zaragosi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zaragosi et al., 2010.

claim: Eliminating senescent cells from naturally-aged INK-ATTAC mice reduced activin A.
source: Eliminating senescent cells from naturally-aged INK-ATTAC mice reduced activin A and increased adipose tissue C/EBPα and PPARγ.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4e,f showing reduced activin A in plasma and adipose tissue.

claim: Eliminating senescent cells from naturally-aged INK-ATTAC mice increased adipose tissue C/EBPα and PPARγ.
source: Eliminating senescent cells from naturally-aged INK-ATTAC mice reduced activin A and increased adipose tissue C/EBPα and PPARγ.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4f showing increased C/EBPα and PPARγ expression.

claim: JAK pathway inhibition suppressed production of activin A by senescent fat progenitors.
source: JAK pathway inhibition suppressed production of activin A by senescent fat progenitors and partially rescued adipogenic capacity both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5a,b showing reduced activin A in JAK inhibitor-treated senescent cells.

claim: JAK pathway inhibition partially rescued adipogenic capacity both in vitro and in vivo.
source: JAK pathway inhibition suppressed production of activin A by senescent fat progenitors and partially rescued adipogenic capacity both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5c,d (in vitro) and Figure 7b (in vivo) showing improved adipogenic markers.

claim: JAK inhibition in aged mice reduced lipotoxicity.
source: JAK inhibition in aged mice reduced lipotoxicity and increased insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7e,f,g showing reduced plasma FFA and hepatic triglycerides.

claim: JAK inhibition in aged mice increased insulin sensitivity.
source: JAK inhibition in aged mice reduced lipotoxicity and increased insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8d,e showing improved insulin tolerance.

claim: Primary cells were isolated from the stromal-vascular fraction of collagenase-digested subcutaneous fat from healthy human subjects undergoing surgery to donate a kidney.
source: Primary cells were isolated from the stromal-vascular fraction of collagenase-digested subcutaneous fat from healthy human subjects undergoing surgery to donate a kidney.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Cells exposed to 10 Gy irradiation had at least 70% of cells become SABG-positive within 20 days.
source: These cells were exposed to 10 Gy irradiation, which induced at least 70% of cells to become senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SABG) -positive within 20 days, as previously described (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Senescent source cells were less differentiated than control non-senescent source cells.
source: We found that senescent source cells were less differentiated than control non-senescent source cells (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by visual evidence in Figure 1a showing fewer lipid-containing cells in senescent cultures.

claim: When co-cultured with senescent source cells, only 20% of target progenitors accumulated lipid compared to more than 50% when co-cultured with non-senescent source cells.
source: When co-cultured with senescent source cells, only 20% of target progenitors accumulated lipid compared to more than 50% when co-cultured with non-senescent source cells (Figure 1b)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Senescent cells can directly impair lipid accumulation by nearby fat progenitors.
source: When co-cultured with senescent source cells, only 20% of target progenitors accumulated lipid compared to more than 50% when co-cultured with non-senescent source cells (Figure 1b), indicating that senescent cells can directly impair lipid accumulation by nearby fat progenitors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-culture experiment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Senescent progenitor CM reduced differentiated cell numbers in target non-senescent cells at all three time points tested.
source: Senescent progenitor CM reduced differentiated cell numbers in target non-senescent cells at all three time points tested (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by visual evidence in Figure 2a showing reduced lipid accumulation at days 5, 10, and 15.

claim: Differentiation-dependent expression of PPARγ, C/EBPα, FABP4, and PLIN2 was blunted by CM from senescent cells compared to CM from blank culture flasks or control non-senescent cells.
source: Differentiation-dependent expression of these genes was blunted by CM from senescent cells compared to CM from blank culture flasks or control non-senescent cells (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Cellular senescence did not appear to be induced in the target cells by the 15 days of CM exposure.
source: Cellular senescence did not appear to be induced in the target cells by the 15 days of CM exposure, since p16Ink4a and Cdkn1a (p21Cip) transcript levels were not increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a showing no increase in senescence markers.

claim: Adipogenesis was not impaired when exposure to CM was limited to 24 hours of pretreatment before exposure to DM.
source: Adipogenesis was not impaired when exposure to CM was limited to 24 hours of pretreatment before exposure to DM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Impaired adipogenesis due to senescent CM depends on continued presence of products secreted by senescent cells.
source: This suggests that impaired adipogenesis due to senescent CM depends on continued presence of products secreted by senescent cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that 24-hour pretreatment was insufficient to impair adipogenesis.

claim: CM from doxorubicin-induced senescent cells suppressed adipogenesis similarly to CM from irradiation-induced senescent cells.
source: CM from doxorubicin-induced senescent cells suppressed adipogenesis similarly to CM from irradiation-induced senescent cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: CM from senescent cells inhibited adipogenesis even after freeze-thaw cycles.
source: We found that CM from senescent cells inhibited adipogenesis even after freeze-thaw cycles (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2a,b showing continued inhibition of adipogenesis.

claim: Cell-cell contact or molecules with short half-lives do not appear to be the sole responsible factors for impaired adipogenesis.
source: Therefore, cell-cell contact or molecules with short half-lives, including many metabolites such as reactive oxygen species (ROS), do not appear to be the sole responsible factors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that CM remains active after freeze-thaw cycles.

claim: The fraction of CM from senescent cells larger than ~10kd impaired adipogenesis while the fraction smaller than ~10kd had no effect.
source: The fraction larger than ~10kd impaired adipogenesis while the fraction smaller than ~10kd had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: SB-431542, an activin A receptor inhibitor, substantially improved adipogenesis in progenitors exposed to CM from senescent cells.
source: Among the compounds screened, SB-431542, an activin A receptor inhibitor (Inman et al., 2002) , substantially improved adipogenesis in progenitors exposed to CM from senescent cells, while only slightly increasing adipogenesis in control cells (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is supported by visual and gene expression data in Figure 3a,b.

claim: SB-431542 only slightly increased adipogenesis in control cells.
source: Among the compounds screened, SB-431542, an activin A receptor inhibitor (Inman et al., 2002) , substantially improved adipogenesis in progenitors exposed to CM from senescent cells, while only slightly increasing adipogenesis in control cells (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3a,b.

claim: Activin A-specific neutralizing antibody enhanced adipogenesis in cells exposed to senescent CM.
source: Due to the fact that SB-431542 also inhibits TGFβ signaling (Inman et al., 2002) , to confirm further the role of activin A, we used activin A-specific neutralizing antibody and observed a similar enhancement of adipogenesis (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This is supported by visual and gene expression data in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Activin A plays a role in the impairment of adipogenesis by senescent cells.
source: Together, these findings indicate that activin A plays a role in the impairment of adipogenesis by senescent cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rescue experiments with SB-431542 and activin A neutralizing antibody.

claim: After 17–18 months-of-age, mice begin to lose fat mass.
source: After 17–18 months-of-age, mice begin to lose fat mass.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and is consistent with data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Senescent cells start to accumulate noticeably before 18 months-of-age in mouse fat tissue.
source: We previously found that senescent cells start to accumulate noticeably before 18 months-of-age in mouse fat tissue (Stout et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stout et al., 2014.

claim: Senescent cells play a role in age-related loss of subcutaneous fat in animals with progeria.
source: We previously found that senescent cells start to accumulate noticeably before 18 months-of-age in mouse fat tissue (Stout et al., 2014) and senescent cells play a role in age-related loss of subcutaneous fat in animals with progeria (Baker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baker et al., 2011.

claim: During the three-week treatment period, WT mice lost more fat than INK-ATTAC+/- mice.
source: During the three-week treatment period, WT mice lost more fat than INK-ATTAC+/- mice (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4a showing differential fat loss between groups.

claim: Lean mass and total body weight were unaffected by senescent cell clearance in 18-month-old INK-ATTAC mice.
source: During the three-week treatment period, WT mice lost more fat than INK-ATTAC+/- mice (Figure 4a), while lean mass (Figure 4b) and total body weight (Figure 4c) were unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4b,c showing no significant differences in lean mass or body weight.

claim: Circulating activin A was reduced more than 30% compared to baseline in the INK-ATTAC+/- mice.
source: Circulating activin A was reduced more than 30% compared to baseline in the INK-ATTAC+/- mice, while activin A increased by 10% in the WT group (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4e showing changes in plasma activin A levels.

claim: Activin A increased by 10% in the WT group during the three-week treatment period.
source: Circulating activin A was reduced more than 30% compared to baseline in the INK-ATTAC+/- mice, while activin A increased by 10% in the WT group (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4e.

claim: Activin A was reduced in adipose tissue of the INK-ATTAC+/- mice.
source: Activin A was also reduced in adipose tissue of the INK-ATTAC+/- mice (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 4f.

claim: Adipose tissue expression of C/EBPα and PPARγ was higher in the INK-ATTAC+/- than WT mice.
source: Adipose tissue expression of C/EBPα and PPARγ was higher in he INK-ATTAC+/- than WT mice (Figure 4f), indicative of improved adipogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 4f.

claim: Lipin-1 expression in fat tissue is positively associated with adipose tissue function.
source: Lipin-1, whose expression in fat tissue is positively associated with adipose tissue function (Nadra et al., 2012) and insulin sensitivity (Donkor et al., 2008) , was also increased in the INK-ATTAC+/- mice (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nadra et al., 2012 and Donkor et al., 2008.

claim: Lipin-1 expression in fat tissue is positively associated with insulin sensitivity.
source: Lipin-1, whose expression in fat tissue is positively associated with adipose tissue function (Nadra et al., 2012) and insulin sensitivity (Donkor et al., 2008) , was also increased in the INK-ATTAC+/- mice (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Donkor et al., 2008.

claim: Lipin-1 was increased in the INK-ATTAC+/- mice after senescent cell clearance.
source: Lipin-1, whose expression in fat tissue is positively associated with adipose tissue function (Nadra et al., 2012) and insulin sensitivity (Donkor et al., 2008) , was also increased in the INK-ATTAC+/- mice (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 4f.

claim: The senescence markers IL6, p16Ink4a, and p21Cip1 were reduced in fat tissue of AP20187-treated INK-ATTAC+/- mice.
source: The senescence markers, IL6, p16Ink4a, and p21Cip1 (Figure 4f) as well as SABG+ cells (Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), were reduced in fat tissue of AP20187-treated INK-ATTAC+/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 4f and SABG staining in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SABG+ cells were reduced in fat tissue of AP20187-treated INK-ATTAC+/- mice.
source: The senescence markers, IL6, p16Ink4a, and p21Cip1 (Figure 4f) as well as SABG+ cells (Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), were reduced in fat tissue of AP20187-treated INK-ATTAC+/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 4d and images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Senescent cells are a cause of age-related adipose tissue loss and dysfunction in older mice.
source: These results suggest that senescent cells are a cause of age-related adipose tissue loss and dysfunction in older mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the INK-ATTAC mouse experiments showing that clearing senescent cells prevents fat loss and improves adipogenic markers.

claim: JAK inhibition reduces activin A at both the transcript and secreted protein levels in senescent fat progenitors.
source: Here, we found that JAK inhibition reduces activin A at both the transcript (Figure 5a) and secreted protein levels (Figure 5b) in senescent fat progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression and ELISA data in Figure 5a,b.

claim: CM prepared from senescent progenitors exposed to JAK inhibitor caused less inhibition of adipogenesis in non-senescent target progenitors than CM prepared from senescent cells exposed to vehicle.
source: CM prepared from senescent progenitors exposed to JAK inhibitor caused less inhibition of adipogenesis in non-senescent target progenitors than CM prepared from senescent cells exposed to vehicle (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: This is supported by visual and gene expression data in Figure 5c,d.

claim: Addition of JAK inhibitor directly to CM previously collected from either control or senescent cells did not affect adipogenesis in the target non-senescent cells.
source: Addition of JAK inhibitor directly to CM previously collected from either control or senescent cells did not affect adipogenesis in the target non-senescent cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: JAK inhibitor alleviated impaired adipogenesis mainly by acting on the senescent source fat progenitors, rather than having direct effects on the target cells.
source: This indicates that JAK inhibitor alleviated impaired adipogenesis mainly by acting on the senescent source fat progenitors, in turn altering the composition of the CM, rather than having direct effects on the target cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that adding JAK inhibitor directly to CM had no effect.

claim: JAK inhibition improved adipogenesis in cultures of fat progenitors isolated from aged rats, which contain senescent cells.
source: Moreover, JAK inhibition improved adipogenesis in cultures of fat progenitors isolated from aged rats, which contain senescent cells, but not in cultured progenitors isolated from young rats (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by visual and gene expression data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: JAK inhibition did not improve adipogenesis in cultured progenitors isolated from young rats.
source: Moreover, JAK inhibition improved adipogenesis in cultures of fat progenitors isolated from aged rats, which contain senescent cells, but not in cultured progenitors isolated from young rats (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: Vehicle-treated 22-24 month-old mice progressively lost fat over two months.
source: Vehicle-treated mice progressively lost fat over two months, while JAK inhibitor administration prevented this age-related fat loss (Figure 6a,d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6a,d showing progressive fat loss in control mice.

claim: JAK inhibitor administration prevented age-related fat loss in 22-24 month-old mice.
source: Vehicle-treated mice progressively lost fat over two months, while JAK inhibitor administration prevented this age-related fat loss (Figure 6a,d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6a,d showing preserved fat mass in ruxolitinib-treated mice.

claim: The lean mass of both vehicle and ruxolitinib-treated groups remained unchanged.
source: The lean mass of both groups remained unchanged (Figure 6b,e).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6b,e showing no change in lean mass.

claim: The body weights of the vehicle-treated compared to the INCB-treated mice was not significantly different.
source: The body weights of the vehicle-treated compared to the INCB-treated mice was not significantly different (Figure 6c,f).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6c,f showing no significant difference in body weight.

claim: The same INCB treatment only exhibited a non-significant trend to alter fat mass in young (8-month-old) mice.
source: The same INCB treatment only exhibited a non-significant trend to alter fat mass in young (8-month-old) mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Inguinal, subscapular, and brown fat mass were reduced in the vehicle-treated group, but were preserved in INCB-treated mice.
source: Inguinal, subscapular, and brown fat mass were reduced in the vehicle-treated group, but were preserved in INCB-treated mice (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7a showing fat depot weights.

claim: JAK inhibition increased adipose tissue transcript levels of PPARγ, C/EBPα, FABP4, and adipo-Q in aged mice.
source: JAK inhibition increased adipose tissue transcript levels of the adipogenesis markers, PPARγ, C/EBPα, FABP4, and adipo-Q, as well as GPAT4 (glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase isoform-4, a TG synthesis marker) (Figure 7b)
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 7b.

claim: JAK inhibition increased adipose tissue transcript levels of GPAT4 in aged mice.
source: JAK inhibition increased adipose tissue transcript levels of the adipogenesis markers, PPARγ, C/EBPα, FABP4, and adipo-Q, as well as GPAT4 (glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase isoform-4, a TG synthesis marker) (Figure 7b)
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 7b.

claim: JAK inhibition may act by enhancing adipogenesis and increasing TG storage in fat in aged mice.
source: JAK inhibition increased adipose tissue transcript levels of the adipogenesis markers, PPARγ, C/EBPα, FABP4, and adipo-Q, as well as GPAT4 (glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase isoform-4, a TG synthesis marker) (Figure 7b), suggesting that JAK inhibition may act by enhancing adipogenesis and increasing TG storage in fat in aged mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data showing increased adipogenic and TG synthesis markers.

claim: Lipin-1 was increased in fat tissue from JAK inhibitor-treated mice.
source: Lipin-1 was also increased in fat tissue from JAK inhibitor-treated mice (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 7b.

claim: Activin A increased with aging in both fat tissues and the circulation.
source: Activin A increased with aging in both fat tissues (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c) and the circulation (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c and Figure 7c comparing young and old mice.

claim: JAK inhibition suppressed activin A in whole fat of aged mice.
source: JAK inhibition suppressed activin A in both whole fat (Figure 7b) and progenitors isolated from fat tissue (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), as well as circulating activin A (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 7b.

claim: JAK inhibition suppressed activin A in progenitors isolated from fat tissue of aged mice.
source: JAK inhibition suppressed activin A in both whole fat (Figure 7b) and progenitors isolated from fat tissue (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), as well as circulating activin A (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: JAK inhibition suppressed circulating activin A in aged mice.
source: JAK inhibition suppressed activin A in both whole fat (Figure 7b) and progenitors isolated from fat tissue (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), as well as circulating activin A (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 7c.

claim: JAK inhibition did not reduce activin A expression in fat tissue of younger (8-month old) mice.
source: Notably, JAK inhibition did not reduce activin A expression or improve adipogenesis in fat tissue of younger (8-month old) mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b.

claim: JAK inhibition did not improve adipogenesis in fat tissue of younger (8-month old) mice.
source: Notably, JAK inhibition did not reduce activin A expression or improve adipogenesis in fat tissue of younger (8-month old) mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Administering JAK inhibitor did not change metabolic rate in aged mice.
source: Administering JAK inhibitor did not change metabolic rate or food intake in aged mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by CLAMS data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Administering JAK inhibitor did not change food intake in aged mice.
source: Administering JAK inhibitor did not change metabolic rate or food intake in aged mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by CLAMS data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: JAK inhibitor was previously found to increase activity of old mice.
source: Administering JAK inhibitor did not change metabolic rate or food intake in aged mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and was previously found by us to actually increase activity of old mice (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: Expression of ATGL and HSL was induced in fat tissue by JAK inhibition.
source: Expression of two lipolytic enzymes, adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL) and hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL), was induced in fat tissue by JAK inhibition (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 7b.

claim: The fat maintenance observed with JAK inhibition was not due to increased food intake, decreased energy expenditure, or decreased lipolysis.
source: This suggests that the fat maintenance we observed was not due to increased food intake, decreased energy expenditure, or decreased lipolysis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the metabolic rate, food intake, and lipolytic enzyme expression data.

claim: Plasma free fatty acid levels were reduced by JAK inhibitor in aged mice.
source: Plasma free fatty acid (FFA) levels were reduced by JAK inhibitor (Figure 7e)
evidence: This is supported by FFA measurement data in Figure 7e.

claim: Plasma TG was not different between vehicle and JAK inhibitor-treated aged mice.
source: Plasma free fatty acid (FFA) levels were reduced by JAK inhibitor (Figure 7e), while TG was not different (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is supported by TG measurement data in Figure 7d.

claim: JAK inhibitor decreased liver weight in old mice.
source: In addition, JAK inhibitor decreased both liver weight (Figure 7a) and hepatic TG (Figure 7f,g) in old mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7a showing liver weight as percent of body weight.

claim: JAK inhibitor decreased hepatic TG in old mice.
source: In addition, JAK inhibitor decreased both liver weight (Figure 7a) and hepatic TG (Figure 7f,g) in old mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7f,g showing hepatic TG measurements.

claim: Lipotoxicity and decreased adipogenic capacity are associated with insulin resistance.
source: Lipotoxicity and decreased adipogenic capacity are associated with insulin resistance (Wang et al., 2008; Unger and Scherer, 2010; Gustafson et al., 2015; Tchkonia et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Insulin sensitivity was impaired in 22-month- compared to 8-month-old mice.
source: By conducting glucose and insulin tolerance tests, we found that insulin sensitivity was impaired in 22-month- compared to 8-month-old mice (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is supported by insulin tolerance test data in Figure 8e.

claim: JAK inhibitor improved glucose homeostasis in 22-month-old mice.
source: JAK inhibitor improved glucose homeostasis (Figure 8a,b) and insulin sensitivity (Figure 8d,e) in 22-month-old mice
evidence: This is supported by glucose tolerance test data in Figure 8a,b.

claim: JAK inhibitor improved insulin sensitivity in 22-month-old mice.
source: JAK inhibitor improved glucose homeostasis (Figure 8a,b) and insulin sensitivity (Figure 8d,e) in 22-month-old mice
evidence: This is supported by insulin tolerance test data in Figure 8d,e.

claim: JAK inhibitor had little effect on glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity in young mice.
source: JAK inhibitor improved glucose homeostasis (Figure 8a,b) and insulin sensitivity (Figure 8d,e) in 22-month-old mice, while it had little effect in young mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glucose-stimulated insulin secretion capacity was not altered by JAK inhibition in 22-month-old mice.
source: Glucose-stimulated insulin secretion capacity was not altered by JAK inhibition in 22-month-old mice (Figure 8c)
evidence: This is supported by insulin secretion data in Figure 8c.

claim: Pancreatic islet function might not be affected by JAK inhibition.
source: Glucose-stimulated insulin secretion capacity was not altered by JAK inhibition in 22-month-old mice (Figure 8c), suggesting that pancreatic islet function might not be affected.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the glucose-stimulated insulin secretion data.

claim: Fasting glucose was unchanged with JAK inhibitor treatment.
source: Fasting glucose was also unchanged with JAK inhibitor treatment (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8f (note: there appears to be a discrepancy in the figure reference).

claim: Fat tissue isolated from the JAK inhibitor-treated group exhibited more robust induction of p-AKT in response to insulin compared to the control group.
source: To test whether insulin sensitivity in fat tissue of aged mice was improved by JAK inhibitor, we performed an ex vivo insulin challenge test and found that fat tissue isolated from the JAK inhibitor-treated group exhibited more robust induction of p-AKT in response to insulin compared to the control group (Figure 8g,h).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 8g,h showing increased p-AKT/total AKT ratio.

claim: Improved fat tissue function through JAK inhibition possibly contributed to enhanced insulin sensitivity in aged mice.
source: Therefore, it appears that improved fat tissue function through JAK inhibition possibly contributed to enhanced insulin sensitivity in aged mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ex vivo insulin challenge data and other metabolic measurements.

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway plays an important role in adipose tissue development and function.
source: The JAK/STAT pathway plays an important role in adipose tissue development and function (Richard and Stephens, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: JAK inhibitor treatment inhibited production of SASP factors in aged mice.
source: Previously, we found that JAK inhibitor treatment inhibited production of SASP factors and improved physical function in aged mice (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: JAK inhibitor treatment improved physical function in aged mice.
source: Previously, we found that JAK inhibitor treatment inhibited production of SASP factors and improved physical function in aged mice (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: JAK1/2 inhibition has metabolic benefits in aged mice.
source: Here, we show that JAK1/2 inhibition has metabolic benefits in aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing improved glucose homeostasis, insulin sensitivity, and reduced lipotoxicity.

claim: JAK inhibitor treatment suppressed activin A production by senescent cells in vitro.
source: JAK inhibitor treatment suppressed activin A production by senescent cells in vitro and in fat progenitors, fat tissue, and the circulation in aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5a,b.

claim: JAK inhibitor treatment suppressed activin A in fat progenitors in aged mice.
source: JAK inhibitor treatment suppressed activin A production by senescent cells in vitro and in fat progenitors, fat tissue, and the circulation in aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: JAK inhibitor treatment suppressed activin A in fat tissue in aged mice.
source: JAK inhibitor treatment suppressed activin A production by senescent cells in vitro and in fat progenitors, fat tissue, and the circulation in aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7b.

claim: JAK inhibitor treatment suppressed activin A in the circulation in aged mice.
source: JAK inhibitor treatment suppressed activin A production by senescent cells in vitro and in fat progenitors, fat tissue, and the circulation in aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7c.

claim: One possible mechanism for improved adipogenesis and fat tissue function by JAK inhibitor treatment is reduction of activin A production by senescent cells.
source: One possible mechanism for improved adipogenesis and fat tissue function by JAK inhibitor treatment is reduction of activin A production by senescent cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the correlation between reduced activin A and improved adipogenesis.

claim: Other SASP components (i.e. IL-6, TNFα, and IFNγ) may also contribute to impairment of adipose tissue function in aged animals.
source: Other SASP components (i.e. IL-6, TNFα, and IFNγ) may also contribute to impairment of adipose tissue function in aged animals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging other potential mechanisms.

claim: Mechanisms other than those directly affecting senescent cells may have contributed to the improved adipogenesis.
source: It is possible that mechanisms other than those directly affecting senescent cells contributed to the improved adipogenesis we found.
evidence: This is a speculative acknowledgment of potential alternative mechanisms.

claim: Senescent cells of many types and in multiple tissues are likely affected by systemic administration of JAK1/2 inhibitors to mice or AP20187 to INK-ATTAC animals.
source: Also, senescent cells of many types and in multiple tissues, not only in fat, are likely affected by systemic administration of JAK1/2 inhibitors to mice or AP20187 to INK-ATTAC animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the systemic nature of the treatments.

claim: Systemic effects of JAK inhibitors and AP20187 likely contributed to alleviating metabolic dysfunction.
source: Very likely, these systemic effects of our interventions contributed to alleviating metabolic dysfunction.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the contribution of systemic effects.

claim: Young mice have fewer senescent cells than old mice.
source: To partially address this, rather than conducting an epistasis experiment (treating senescent cell-depleted INK-ATTAC mice with JAK inhibitor to check for off-target effects), we compared effects of JAK inhibitor treatment in old to young mice, since the latter have fewer senescent cells, like AP20187-treated INK-ATTAC mice.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is consistent with prior data showing senescent cell accumulation with age.

claim: More than 50% of senescent cells can remain after treatment with AP20187 in INK-ATTAC mice.
source: The lack of substantial effects of JAK inhibitor treatment on adipogenesis, fat depot weights, and insulin sensitivity in young animals, but strong effects in old animals with higher senescent cell burden and activin A, coupled with parallel effects between JAK inhibitor treatment in wild type mice to those of genetic clearance with AP20187 in INK-ATTAC mice, suggest that effects of JAK inhibitors on senescent cells may contribute to improved metabolic function in older mice.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Effects of JAK inhibitors on senescent cells may contribute to improved metabolic function in older mice.
source: The lack of substantial effects of JAK inhibitor treatment on adipogenesis, fat depot weights, and insulin sensitivity in young animals, but strong effects in old animals with higher senescent cell burden and activin A, coupled with parallel effects between JAK inhibitor treatment in wild type mice to those of genetic clearance with AP20187 in INK-ATTAC mice, suggest that effects of JAK inhibitors on senescent cells may contribute to improved metabolic function in older mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing effects in young versus old mice and JAK inhibitor versus genetic clearance.

claim: Impaired adipogenesis leads to ectopic lipid accumulation and insulin resistance.
source: Our findings are consistent with the speculation that impaired adipogenesis leads to ectopic lipid accumulation and insulin resistance (Gustafson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation and the authors' data showing reduced ectopic lipids and improved insulin sensitivity with improved adipogenesis.

claim: JAK pathway inhibition led to maintained fat mass and enhanced metabolic function in tandem with improved adipogenic capacity in aged mice.
source: We found that JAK pathway inhibition led to maintained fat mass and enhanced metabolic function in tandem with improved adipogenic capacity in aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by data showing preserved fat mass, improved insulin sensitivity, and increased adipogenic markers.

claim: PPARγ and C/EBPα are essential for insulin sensitivity.
source: Expression of PPARγ and C/EBPα, both of which are essential for insulin sensitivity (Wu et al., 1999; El-Jack et al., 1999) , increased in adipose tissue of JAK inhibitor-treated mice.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Expression of PPARγ and C/EBPα increased in adipose tissue of JAK inhibitor-treated mice.
source: Expression of PPARγ and C/EBPα, both of which are essential for insulin sensitivity (Wu et al., 1999; El-Jack et al., 1999) , increased in adipose tissue of JAK inhibitor-treated mice.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 7b.

claim: Reduced circulating FFAs and hepatic lipid accumulation are important manifestations of lipotoxicity associated with insulin resistance.
source: These changes were accompanied by reduced circulating FFAs and hepatic lipid accumulation, two important manifestations of lipotoxicity associated with insulin resistance (Slawik and Vidal-Puig, 2006; Boden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: JAK inhibition reduces systemic inflammation in aged mice.
source: In addition to improved adipogenesis, JAK inhibition reduces systemic inflammation (including reducing circulating IL6) in aged mice (Xu et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: JAK inhibition promotes 'browning' of adipose tissue.
source: In addition to improved adipogenesis, JAK inhibition reduces systemic inflammation (including reducing circulating IL6) in aged mice (Xu et al., 2015) and promotes 'browning' of adipose tissue (Moisan et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moisan et al., 2015.

claim: Reduced inflammation and browning of adipose tissue are known to affect adipogenesis and insulin sensitivity.
source: In addition to improved adipogenesis, JAK inhibition reduces systemic inflammation (including reducing circulating IL6) in aged mice (Xu et al., 2015) and promotes 'browning' of adipose tissue (Moisan et al., 2015) , both of which are known to affect adipogenesis and insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Reduced inflammation and browning might contribute to improved insulin sensitivity in aged mice in addition to reduced activin A level.
source: These mechanisms might also contribute to improved insulin sensitivity in aged mice in addition to reduced activin A level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential contributing mechanisms.

claim: JAK inhibition improved adipogenesis and insulin sensitivity in aged mice but did so much less in younger mice.
source: Importantly, JAK inhibition improved adipogenesis and insulin sensitivity in aged mice but did so much less in younger mice
evidence: This is supported by data comparing effects in old versus young mice.

claim: The JAK pathway participates in age- or senescence-related pathogenesis of adipose tissue dysfunction.
source: Importantly, JAK inhibition improved adipogenesis and insulin sensitivity in aged mice but did so much less in younger mice, suggesting that the JAK pathway participates in age- or senescence-related pathogenesis of adipose tissue dysfunction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects in young versus old mice.

claim: The effects of JAK inhibitors seem to be similar in mouse, rat, and human models.
source: Furthermore, the effects of JAK inhibitors seem to be similar in mouse, rat, and human models.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing similar effects across species.

claim: The most fundamental aging mechanisms are conserved across mammalian species.
source: This is consistent with the speculation that the most fundamental aging mechanisms are conserved across mammalian species.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary conservation of aging mechanisms.

claim: Activin A is involved in a variety of biological events.
source: Activin A is a member of the transforming growth factor superfamily and is involved in a variety of biological events (Xia and Schneyer, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Activin A has widespread effects on multiple types of progenitors.
source: Activin A has widespread effects on multiple types of progenitors (Zaragosi et al., 2010; Bowser et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Activin A interacts with the closely related growth and differentiation factors (GDFs), which share receptor and signaling mechanisms with activin A.
source: Activin A has widespread effects on multiple types of progenitors (Zaragosi et al., 2010; Bowser et al., 2013) both directly and through interaction with the closely related growth and differentiation factors (GDFs), which share receptor and signaling mechanisms with activin A (Sako et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sako et al., 2010 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Circulating activin A levels could be a bio-marker of senescent cell burden.
source: Our results suggest that circulating activin A levels could be a bio-marker of senescent cell burden
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the correlations observed in the study.

claim: Circulating levels of activin A increase with aging.
source: Our results suggest that circulating activin A levels could be a bio-marker of senescent cell burden since: 1) circulating levels of activin A increase with aging, consistent with the increase in senescent cell abundance with aging
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7c comparing young and old mice.

claim: Senescent cells secrete activin A.
source: Our results suggest that circulating activin A levels could be a bio-marker of senescent cell burden since: 1) circulating levels of activin A increase with aging, consistent with the increase in senescent cell abundance with aging, 2) senescent cells secrete activin A
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5a,b showing increased activin A in senescent cells.

claim: Genetic clearance of senescent cells from 18-month-old INK-ATTAC+/- mice reduced circulating activin A.
source: Our results suggest that circulating activin A levels could be a bio-marker of senescent cell burden since: 1) circulating levels of activin A increase with aging, consistent with the increase in senescent cell abundance with aging, 2) senescent cells secrete activin A, 3) genetic clearance of senescent cells from 18-month-old INK-ATTAC+/- mice reduced circulating activin A
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4e.

claim: JAK inhibition suppresses activin A production in senescent cells in vitro and in aged mice in vivo.
source: Our results suggest that circulating activin A levels could be a bio-marker of senescent cell burden since: 1) circulating levels of activin A increase with aging, consistent with the increase in senescent cell abundance with aging, 2) senescent cells secrete activin A, 3) genetic clearance of senescent cells from 18-month-old INK-ATTAC+/- mice reduced circulating activin A, and 4) JAK inhibition suppresses activin A production in senescent cells in vitro and in aged mice in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: A variety of cell types can regulate activin A production, including macrophages.
source: It is important to note that a variety of cell types can regulate activin A production, including macrophages (Zaragosi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Cell types other than senescent cells may contribute to increased activin A levels with aging.
source: It is possible that these cell types contribute to increased activin A levels with aging.
evidence: This is a speculative acknowledgment of potential alternative sources of activin A.

claim: Most activin A-blocking agents such as follistatin also inhibit myostatin due to structural similarity to activin A.
source: However, most activin A-blocking agents such as follistatin also inhibit myostatin due to structural similarity to activin A (Cash et al., 2009; Nakatani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Activin A-blocking agents would be anticipated to alter both muscle and fat mass though additional mechanisms that may be independent of activin A.
source: These agents would therefore be anticipated to alter both muscle and fat mass though additional mechanisms that may be independent of activin A (Lee, 2004; McPherron and Lee, 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known effects of myostatin inhibition, supported by citations.

claim: JAK inhibitor treatment did not alter lean mass in aged mice.
source: JAK inhibitor treatment did not alter lean mass in aged mice (Figure 6b,e).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6b,e.

claim: JAK inhibition might be superior to current activin A-blocking agents for alleviation of age-related adipose tissue dysfunction.
source: Thus, JAK inhibition might be superior to current activin A-blocking agents for alleviation of age-related adipose tissue dysfunction.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the selective effects of JAK inhibitors on fat mass without affecting lean mass.

claim: Ruxolitinib is approved by FDA for treating myelofibrosis.
source: Ruxolitinib, the JAK1/2 inhibitor we used in vivo, is approved by FDA for treating myelofibrosis (Verstovsek et al., 2010; Harrison et al., 2012; Verstovsek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Ruxolitinib has side-effects in human subjects with myelofibrosis including anemia and thrombocytopenia.
source: Although it has side-effects in human subjects with myelofibrosis including anemia and thrombocytopenia (Verstovsek et al., 2010; Verstovsek et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Ruxolitinib has minimal effects on peripheral blood cell populations in both young and old mice.
source: Although it has side-effects in human subjects with myelofibrosis including anemia and thrombocytopenia (Verstovsek et al., 2010; Verstovsek et al., 2012) , we and others found that ruxolitinib has minimal effects on peripheral blood cell populations in both young (Quintás-Cardama et al., 2010) and old mice (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Senescent cells can exert profound effects on tissue and organismal function by affecting normal progenitors or stem cells through production of TGFβ family members.
source: Albeit speculative, our findings are consistent with the general hypothesis that senescent cells might exert profound effects on tissue and organismal function by affecting normal progenitors or stem cells through production of TGFβ family members, such as activin A, and potentially other types of factors secreted by senescent cells.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a speculative hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: Targeting senescent cells or their products could be a promising avenue for delaying, preventing, alleviating, or treating age-related stem cell, progenitor, and adipose tissue dysfunction and metabolic disease.
source: Our work suggests that targeting senescent cells or their products could be a promising avenue for delaying, preventing, alleviating, or treating age-related stem cell, progenitor, and adipose tissue dysfunction and metabolic disease.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.
